items.title: "The other two founders were probably there on the decision sooner than I was." Pivots aren't just about changing a business model. They're also about...
items.description_html:
"The other two founders were probably there on the decision sooner than I was."

Pivots aren't just about changing a business model.

They're also about ensuring your co-founders and team are willing to make the leap with you.

But sometimes, they might be ahead of you.

Urban Company co-founder and CEO Abhiraj Singh Bhal says its defining pivot taught him exactly that.

Bhal admits he held on to the marketplace model longer than he should have, partly because he worried about how a revenue decline would be perceived after raising institutional capital.

His co-founders, Varun Khaitan (COO) and Raghav Chandra (CTO), approached it differently.

"Their conviction was simple: if it's the right thing for the customer, we should do it."

This and more in the maiden episode of Legendary Pivots, our new series with SeedToScale by Accel.


Seed2Scale: "We could no longer have our feet in two boats."

@urbancompany_UC had ~100 service categories. Only one was working.

@abhirajbhal on why he shut the rest down and took the company from 100 to 50 overnight.

Two years later, the remaining business had gone from 50 to 600.

items.title: Thanks, Mridul. This screenshot is from 2018, and 8 years later it is dangerously easy to make the past look more obvious than it actually was. I was ...
items.description_html:
Thanks, Mridul. This screenshot is from 2018, and 8 years later it is dangerously easy to make the past look more obvious than it actually was.

I was asking exactly the same question then about Neuland and Syngene: where is the hunger to grow?

There was very little evidence.

Neuland had just had a howler. Its capacities across Unit 1 and Unit 2 were not fungible, something that sounds like an operating detail today but was a serious constraint then. Laurus was barely 2 years into its life as a listed company. I wasn't invested because I simply couldn't see enough evidence of its growth hunger. I first invested in late 2019. Syngene was still predominantly a CRO, with Mangalore under construction.

And here is the part worth remembering.

Of the three, I was most optimistic about Syngene.

Fast forward 8 years, and Syngene turned out to be the dead wood, while Neuland and Laurus, the two where I had greater doubts, became two of my best investments ever.

Today Neuland is more than 50x from that 2018 base. That makes the old questions look prescient. They weren't. They were questions, not predictions.

This is where survivorship bias becomes dangerous. We retrieve the old screenshot of the winner. We remember the doubts we eventually overcame. We connect a few dots and unconsciously rewrite uncertainty as foresight.

What disappears from the story are all the contemporaneous beliefs that did not work, including my much stronger conviction in Syngene.

The lesson isn't that I spotted Neuland early. The lesson is that I didn't know which of the 3 would win.

What mattered was staying curious long enough for evidence to emerge, changing the view as the businesses changed, and allowing management execution rather than my original opinion to decide where conviction eventually belonged.

8 years later, the outcome is obvious.

In 2018, it wasn't :)

Perhaps that is the most useful thing an old screenshot can remind us of.

Our deep conversation on Neuland Labs and those frustrating bad qtrs...

items.title: Bloomberg on Russia's version of Dutch disease: "Instead of oil revenues pulling workers and capital into the energy sector while hollowing out the re...
items.description_html:
Bloomberg on Russia's version of Dutch disease: "Instead of oil revenues pulling workers and capital into the energy sector while hollowing out the rest of the economy, massive military spending is drawing them into defense industries, pushing up labor costs and steadily eroding the competitiveness of civilian businesses."

In a closed economic system, like the global economy, rising wages may be painful for businesses in the short term, but as Michael Kalecki explianed, over the longer term they are not a bad thing. By driving demand for production and by creating incentives for businesses to invest in productivity-enhancing technology, they result in faster production growth that ultimately accommodates not only higher wages but also higher profits.

A problem for Russia (and for other countries that try to raise wages) is that it is a part of a badly-globalized economic system, one in which countries are globally competitive in manufacturing mainly to the extent that they are able to suppress wage growth relative to productivity growth.

When wages in an economy grow relative the productivity, in other words, that may be good for global demand and for global growth, but it makes that economy less competitive in manufacturing, sending more than 100% of the benefits of higher wages to manufacturing to its trade partners.

Russia thus faces the double economic problem not just of an incredibly expensive war, but of rising wages which will further undermine its already-struggling manufacturing sector for the benefit of its trade partners.

Russia is not the example that I would have normally used, but it nonetheless illustrates an important point: the global economy would be much better off with a trade and capital regime that rewards economies that raise wages rather than punish them.

items.title: RT ValueEquity: Every few quarters , I look back at companies that had given 25-30% CAGR growth guidance , which these days companies love to give to ...
items.description_html:
RT ValueEquity
Every few quarters , I look back at companies that had given 25-30% CAGR growth guidance , which these days companies love to give to analysts , because its so easy to come up with imaginary numbers

I personally think a lot of it is a vicious loop ( companies that guide aggressively also attract the type of investors who play these lottery games, and it works for the company and the analyst , can raise funding at higher multiples , can come up with some fictional reports to upgrade the stock ) because the fragility in the world is so high that any small event can disrupt global supply chains and break down business models in a few weeks , the fact being , even businesses after a certain extent do not know the future

So I look at some analysts who take 30% guidance and then model it for 5 years and then come up with some imaginary number and then say is cheap/expensive , which is a classic example of illusion of certainty

When the market is so dynamic , don't fall for the illusion of certainty, it will in most cases disappoint just as a sample if you took 30 companies that had guided for 35-30% CAGR growth , maybe 20 do it in the first year , 15 in the next , but over a 3 year period making forecasts on the basis of guidance is a pretty useless exercise , and its not the companies fault , that's the nature of the game

Now , in my opinion the better approach is : Guidance is not a bad thing to give , I also do track it but there is weightage and it always and always has to be looked at in context , Gauge the probability of execution continuing and understand the market dynamic and assess probability and create a execution -probability matrix , it will be far easier and more rewarding as well

Think in scenarios to valuation today , and the odds of how long an execution cycle lasts in that industry and then does the valuation come in the context of incremental size of profit pool to reverse engineer the growth , in most cases you can tell in less than a minute that this is a high probability case or a pathetic hope based investment

Just my opinion

Every few quarters , I look back at companies that had given 25-30% CAGR growth guidance , which these days companies love to give to analysts , because its so easy to come up with imaginary numbers

I personally think a lot of it is a vicious loop ( companies that guide aggressively also attract the type of investors who play these lottery games, and it works for the company and the analyst , can raise funding at higher multiples , can come up with some fictional reports to upgrade the stock ) because the fragility in the world is so high that any small event can disrupt global supply chains and break down business models in a few weeks , the fact being , even businesses after a certain extent do not know the future

So I look at some analysts who take 30% guidance and then model it for 5 years and then come up with some imaginary number and then say is cheap/expensive , which is a classic example of illusion of certainty

When the market is so dynamic , don't fall for the illusion of certainty, it will in most cases disappoint just as a sample if you took 30 companies that had guided for 35-30% CAGR growth , maybe 20 do it in the first year , 15 in the next , but over a 3 year period making forecasts on the basis of guidance is a pretty useless exercise , and its not the companies fault , that's the nature of the game

Now , in my opinion the better approach is : Guidance is not a bad thing to give , I also do track it but there is weightage and it always and always has to be looked at in context , Gauge the probability of execution continuing and understand the market dynamic and assess probability and create a execution -probability matrix , it will be far easier and more rewarding as well

Think in scenarios to valuation today , and the odds of how long an execution cycle lasts in that industry and then does the valuation come in the context of incremental size of profit pool to reverse engineer the growth , in most cases you can tell in less than a minute that this is a high probability case or a pathetic hope based investment

Just my opinion

The decline was driven by private education and health services, as well as leisure and hospitality, which fell -133,000 and -86,000, respectively.

This was followed by wholesale trade and professional and business services, which declined -74,000 and -71,000, respectively.

Despite the decline, there are still 265,000 more available vacancies than unemployed workers, the 2nd-largest difference since January 2025.

As a result, the ratio of job openings to unemployed workers remains at 1.0, the highest since January 2025.

The labor market is becoming increasingly unstable.

items.title: RT Sebastian Mallaby: Early reaction on @demishassabis stepping back: Demis has been playing the role of Google AI statesman for some time, and Koray ...
items.description_html:
RT Sebastian Mallaby
Early reaction on @demishassabis stepping back:

Demis has been playing the role of Google AI statesman for some time, and Koray Kavukcuoglu has been running Google DeepMind research for some time. So this is a formalization of something that had been happening informally. I doubt it changes how well Google executes on AI, and nor does it justify the market's reaction--Alphabet down 5%.

DeepMind's mission has always been to solve AGI and then use it to solve everything else. The solving AGI piece is pretty much done. The channeling AGI into safe and beneficial outcomes is only just beginning. So it makes sense that Demis is shifting his energy from the research to the social impact.

This isn't out of character. Demis cared about safety enough that he sold DeepMind to Google, not to Facebook, even though Facebook offered more money. He cared enough about safety that he fought a three-year battle with Alphabet to get external oversight over DeepMind's AI deployment. This next chapter of his career is a return to that side of his work.

Meanwhile Demis continues to lead Isomorphic Labs, which gives him an opportunity to show how AI can help humanity via medicine.

Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis is stepping aside https://www.axios.com/2026/08/05/google-deepmind-demis-hassabis-ai

items.title: RT IIT Kharagpur: Small Reforms. Big Impact. A Vision for Viksit Bharat. 🇮🇳 As part of the Platinum Jubilee celebrations of IIT Kharagpur, the I...
items.description_html:
RT IIT Kharagpur
Small Reforms. Big Impact. A Vision for Viksit Bharat. 🇮🇳

As part of the Platinum Jubilee celebrations of IIT Kharagpur, the IIT Kharagpur had the privilege of hosting Shri Sanjeev Sanyal, Member of the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister and Chancellor of the Gokhale Institute of Politics and Economics, for an inspiring interactive session on "The Art of Doing Economic Reforms."

Addressing an audience of 450+ students, alumni, industry leaders, faculty members, researchers, and innovators, Shri Sanyal presented a compelling perspective on India's journey towards Viksit Bharat @2047. He highlighted that transformational national progress is driven not only by landmark structural reforms but also by well-designed process reforms that simplify governance, improve transparency, enhance efficiency, and make institutions more citizen-centric. His insightful case studies demonstrated how thoughtful, incremental improvements can deliver extraordinary outcomes.

The event concluded with an engaging fireside conversation between Prof. Suman Chakraborty, Director, IIT Kharagpur, and Shri Sanjeev Sanyal, exploring the intersections of public policy, innovation, higher education, research, entrepreneurship, and India's long-term development agenda.

The programme was graced by Prof. Siddhartha Mukhopadhyay, Dean, Alumni Affairs, and Prof. Jitendra Mahakud, Head, Department of Humanities & Social Sciences, whose presence underscored the Institute's commitment to fostering meaningful dialogue between academia, industry, and policymakers.

At IIT Kharagpur, conversations like these continue to inspire ideas, shape leaders, and strengthen India's innovation ecosystem.

#IITKharagpur #ResearchPark #PlatinumJubilee #SanjeevSanyal #ViksitBharat2047 #EconomicReforms #PublicPolicy #Innovation #Leadership #Academia #Industry #IndiaGrowth #FutureReadyIndia

items.title: I would make Tordoir's point more broadly. German experiences provide an especially good set of examples on whether it is "innovation" or mercantilist...
items.description_html:
I would make Tordoir's point more broadly. German experiences provide an especially good set of examples on whether it is "innovation" or mercantilist labor policies are more likely to drive manufacturing competitiveness.

Germany switched from small deficits and lower manufacturing competitiveness before 2003-05 to a rapid surge in trade surpluses and competitiveness thereafter. During the late 2010s, however, both once again started to decline.

Given that the 2003-05 labor reforms resulted in a sharp decline in German wages relative to productivity, was the subsequent surge in Germany's manufacturing competitiveness driven by the growing gap between wages and productivity, or was it driven by a sudden increase in German innovation skills and a greater innate German ability to invent more advanced technology?

If the latter, why did it last only a decade or so? By the middle of the 2010s, tight German labor markets resulted in a gradual recovery of wages relative to earlier productivity growth. Was the subsequent gradual loss of Germany's manufacturing competitiveness the result of the closing of the gap between wages and productivity, or did Germans around this time began to lose their ability to innovate and to invent more advanced technology?

The point is that innovation and advancements in technology are important because they cause overall productivity to rise, and they allow certain manufacturing sectors, where the innovation is concentrated, to become relatively more competitive than other manufacturing sectors in that country.

But they do not necessarily lead to all manufacturing sectors in a country becoming more competitive than the manufacturing sectors of that country's trade partners. That only happens when wages in that country are lower relative to productivity than they are in the rest of the world.

Technological innovation is of course a great thing, but while it can explain sectoral trade surpluses, it has never explained systemic trade surpluses.


Sander Tordoir: This speaks to one of the misleading semantic narratives pushed against the China shock 2.0 thesis.

It isn’t simply an “innovation shock” in that Germany just fell behind.

As German production declines faster and harder at Chinas hand, so too will its innovative capacity.

items.title: Kalyan Jewellers Q1FY27 Key insights Cons. REV excluding bullion grew 38% YoY to 10,008 Cr, while PAT increased 32% to 349 Cr India remained the key g...
items.description_html:
Kalyan Jewellers Q1FY27 Key insights

Cons. REV excluding bullion grew 38% YoY to 10,008 Cr, while PAT increased 32% to 349 Cr

India remained the key growth driver, with REV increasing 38% to 8,503 Cr & PAT growing 25% to 321 Cr

Demand remained healthy despite temporary weakness during Adhik Maas

Candere delivered a strong turnaround, with REV more than doubling to 141 Cr & PAT turning positive at 2.1 Cr versus a loss of 10 Cr

Management expects Candere to remain profitable through FY27, with the focus shifting towards improving throughput at existing stores

Recycled gold contributed more than 46% of Q1 REV & crossed 55% in June. Management aims to maintain this share at 55-60%, reducing dependence on imported gold

Higher old gold exchange temporarily diluted margins by around 20-30 bps

However, the company is scaling up its cash for gold business, where gold is purchased below the spot price, making it margin accretive & helping offset the exchange related dilution

India PBT margin moderated to around 5.1% from 5.5-5.6% earlier. Management remains confident of maintaining FY26 PBT margins for the full year

Customs duty benefit was 40 Cr in Q1, with another 60 Cr expected in Q2. A meaningful portion of this benefit is being passed on to customers through exchange offers

It launched a new Tamil Nadu focused regional brand, Akshaya Thanga Maligai. The first showroom will open in Chennai on August 21, followed by four additional stores over the next few months

Non GML debt is expected to be fully repaid by the end of September

Store expansion remains on track. The capital light FOCO model continues to support expansion & improving return ratios.

items.description_html:
MCX - Strong YoY, but Sequential Moderation

Q1FY27 results were strong on a YoY basis

REV grew 88% YoY to 702 Cr, while PAT grew 103% YoY to 413 Cr

However, sequentially there was a sharp moderation as Q4FY26 was an exceptional quarter, so some normalisation was expected

Usually, MCX has seen acceleration from Q4 to Q1 of the next financial year, but this time Q1FY27 was lower than Q4FY26 because Q4 had unusually strong commodity activity & volatility

Base effect will also start playing out from Q3FY27

As the company starts comparing against the stronger quarters of last year, YoY growth rates may start moderating

So near term growth optics may not remain as explosive as earlier quarters

Valuation has also adjusted

P/E has reduced to around 42x after the exceptional increase in earnings

So the stock no longer looks as optically expensive as it did earlier, because earnings have caught up meaningfully

items.description_html:
RT Danny (Dennis) Citrinowicz ,داني سيترينوفيتش
The Necessary Evil

If this is ultimately the agreement that emerges, it may be the least bad option available to the Trump administration under current circumstances, especially given its clear desire to avoid another round of military escalation.

The administration has gradually narrowed its own choices, leaving itself with few attractive options and now to end the confrontation the administration will be forced to lift the maritime blockade and restoring the sanctions waiver that allowed Iranian oil exports. That reality has shaped the negotiations from the beginning.

With the necessary caution, the current trajectory appears to point more toward de-escalation than further escalation, a result that will likely frustrate many in Israel while reassuring most Gulf states, whose top priority remains regional stability.

From day one, it was clear that restoring the Strait of Hormuz to its pre-crisis status would have required either regime change in Iran or a sustained military effort to impose control over the waterway. Neither option was politically or strategically acceptable to Washington, given the enormous costs and long-term commitments they would require.

Sometimes, the least desirable option is the only realistic one.

items.title: RT Pavel Durov: Last night Apple briefly removed Telegram from the AppStore because a user had planted illegal porn in a public chat. Telegram was res...
items.description_html:
RT Pavel Durov
Last night Apple briefly removed Telegram from the AppStore because a user had planted illegal porn in a public chat.

Telegram was restored within hours. But I want to explain what happened — to warn other app developers and help protect online communities from similar attacks.

Because Telegram quickly removes illegal content from public groups using all kinds of moderation tools, the attacker had to resort to a technical trick. He inserted AI-modified illegal content by editing an old message in an active group chat. As a result the content was effectively hidden from the group’s members, preventing them from seeing/reporting it.

The attacker was a takedown extortionist: someone who demands ransom from group owners in exchange for not targeting their communities. These extortionists use automated accounts to plant illegal content in public groups and then report it directly to Apple, attempting to trigger the removal of legitimate communities whose owners refused to pay them.

From a practical standpoint, illegal pornographic content in Telegram’s public groups is not a systemic problem. Our moderation is effective. The fact that attackers must resort to backdated, effectively invisible content and other technical tricks proves this.

⚠️ However, there are two important lessons here for app developers and online communities:

— Extortionists have found a way to manipulate Apple into overreacting. Apple removed Telegram from the App Store before contacting us. This creates a potential systemic risk for every mobile app that hosts user-generated content. If an app used by more than a billion people can be removed from the App Store without prior warning, any app can be.

— The tactics used by takedown extortionists are evolving, putting communities across social platforms at risk. Telegram has extensive experience identifying the tricks used by coordinated reporting gangs and protecting legitimate communities (even when doing so risks our own app being temporarily removed from the App Store). Other platforms may not be equally prepared.

Stay vigilant! ☝️

items.description_html:
RT John Kemp
U.S. oil refiners struggle to satisfy fuel demand amid foreign wars

U.S. oil refiners reported record profits in the second quarter as fuel production in the rest of the world was severely disrupted by the wars between the United States and Iran and between Ukraine and Russia.

Partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz coupled with Ukraine’s intensifying attacks on Russia’s refineries cut fuel output worldwide, raising margins for other refiners still able to operate.

In response, U.S. refiners boosted their exports to a record rate, but were unable to increase output by the same amount, leading to a severe depletion of domestic fuel stocks, especially for gasoline and to a lesser extent diesel ...

RT Sumit Behal
The biggest beneficiaries of the Closing Auction Session were Arbitrage Funds and this is visible in the change of fund NAVs on 3rd August

Arbitrage funds recorded their highest daily return (~0.50%) in history by delivering 8–10 times their average daily returns (~0.05%)

UTI Arbitrage Fund : +0.40%
Tata Arbitrage Fund : 0.43%
SBI Arbitrage Fund : +0.51%
Edelweiss Arb Fund : +0.45%
ICICI Arbitrage Fund : +0.44%
Kotak Arbitrage Fund : +0.48%
HDFC Arbitrage Fund : +0.53%
Aditya Birla Arb Fund : +0.48%
Nippon India Arb Fund : +0.48%
Invesco Arbitrage Fund : +0.42%

7 of 10 funds recorded their highest daily percentage gain in the last decade on the first day of the Closing Auction Session

These funds saw a very rare rise in their net asset values across the category, averaging 0.46%. This was about 7.3 standard deviations higher than their usual daily movement

Arbitrage funds are mutual funds that make money by buying a stock cheaply in the cash market and selling it at a higher price in the derivatives (futures) market at the same time

Fun Fact about Royal Enfield -

During World War II, Royal Enfield produced a small 125cc motorcycle that could be dropped from aircraft by parachute alongside airborne troops. It was called the Flying Flea 🪂🏍️

The bike was lightweight, fitted into a specially designed parachute cradle, and was used to give paratroopers mobility once they landed behind enemy lines.

Fast forward ~80 years…

Royal Enfield has brought the name back for its new electric motorcycle brand — Flying Flea.

So the name isn't some fancy EV marketing exercise.

It's actually a tribute to one of the craziest chapters in Royal Enfield's history!

From being dropped out of an aircraft during WWII → to becoming an EV in 2026.

What a legacy! no reco

items.title: RT Vinay Kesari: Good move, and hope it succeeds! Reality check: This amendment would create an *enabling mechanism* to more easily tweak MDR structur...
items.description_html:
RT Vinay Kesari
Good move, and hope it succeeds!

Reality check: This amendment would create an *enabling mechanism* to more easily tweak MDR structure on UPI and RuPay. Any actual change in MDR would have to come via a separate govt. notification under the PSSA (simpler than an amendment to a law), of which there isn't visibility yet.

Why it's still encouraging: It seems unlikely that time would be spent on such an amendment unless there is real intention to tweak MDR structure. UPI subsidy to payments players has been sharply declining (down ~50% since 2023-24) despite the massive growth in UPI and attendant increase in costs. It is inevitable that these costs have to at least be offset if there is to be continued healthy growth of UPI.

What form this could take: Reintroduction of MDR on UPI and RuPay debit txns for 'large merchants' (which industry has been pushing for) is a possible pragmatic path, preserving the benefits of widespread digital acceptance by small merchants while placing the onus on larger merchants to pay for the benefit of frictionless payments.

Qns. to think about: 1. If the eventual notification imposes MDR on txns>Rs.2,000 at large merchants, which payments players would benefit the most in the short term?

2. If the costs related to UPI acceptance for large merchants goes up, it narrows the gap with accepting credit instruments. Could this incentivise more merchant-funded checkout finance?


Pratik Bhakta: Govt is planning to introduce an ammendment to the Payment and Settlement System Act, 2007 thtough Bill no 150 of 2026.

This might pave the way for the RBI to re-impose MDR on RuPay debit cards and UPI.

Sources say bill might be introduced in the Parliament tomorrow.

items.title: RT Vaibhav Bodana: Captain Santosh Kumar, a retired Army officer who noticed something wrong the moment he came home. He returned to Muthanallur in An...
items.description_html:
RT Vaibhav Bodana
Captain Santosh Kumar,
a retired Army officer who noticed something wrong the moment he came home.

He returned to Muthanallur in Anekal Taluk after retiring from the Army in 2008. Every monsoon, roads flooded while nearby lakes stayed dry, and that contradiction bothered him enough to start digging.

He documented lakes and stormwater drains across the taluka and traced the problem to Bengaluru's buried Raja Kaluves between 2017 to 2019. Ancient channels that once moved rainwater from lake to lake. He found British-era maps from 1923 and used them to walk village by village, matching old waterways against what had been built over them.

While studying the link between Muthanallur and Bidaraguppe lakes, he identified four historic Raja Kaluves. One had been so thoroughly encroached that it no longer looked like a waterway at all. Working with residents, he got approvals from the Minor Irrigation Department and restored nearly four kilometres of it, reconnecting it to Battalakere Lake.

The lakes he helped revive are believed to be close to 1,000 years old, some dating back to the reign of Rajaraja Chola I.

This monsoon, neighboring areas flooded again but not Muthanallur.

"In natural settings, rainwater either gets soaked into the soil or makes its way to rain streams, lakes and rivers. If these are maintained efficiently, we will never face floods and calamities." ~ Kumar

The fix already existed, buried under a century of concrete, waiting for someone to go looking with an old map instead of a new budget.

You know the main concern with HAL, it’s not their order book, which is huge. The main concern was order execution. GE is likely to start delivering two jet engines for the Tejas programme in August and another 20 engines by the end of the year.

That should solve the order backlog issue because the aircraft manufacturing bottleneck is solved by HAL

The problem was that GE had stopped manufacturing the GE 404 engine, and they had to restart the manufacturing along with reactivating the entire supply chain, which is now fully active. The Indian GE engine variant is called GE F404-IN20

There are no other ‘manufacturing’ bottlenecks. GE has set up a dedicated line for the Indian variant. HAL has 15 aircraft ready without engines and 6 with engines.

items.description_html:
RT Alec Stapp
Cloudflare is a $100 billion American company with 5,500 employees.

Its president and co-founder is an immigrant who was able to build the company in the US because of Optional Practical Training (OPT).

Here's what she has to say about the program:

“The best thing the U.S. government has done on immigration is OPT to allow international students a chance to stay and work for a time after graduation.”

OPT gave her the opportunity to refine “the business plan that helped create the company."

Charging a $100k fee on OPT would nuke a critical pathway for recruiting & retaining global talent.



Jeremy Neufeld: These immigrant founders of billion-dollar companies first came to the US as students.

A $100,000 fee on OPT would have lost us many of them.

Founders like these would be eligible for an O-1 today, after they've built their companies. But not when they were getting started.

items.title: RT Ajay Rotti: At the outset, I state that the data used and extracted here are correct. I cannot disagree with that. However, I cannot get myself to ...
items.description_html:
RT Ajay Rotti
At the outset, I state that the data used and extracted here are correct. I cannot disagree with that. However, I cannot get myself to agree with the conclusion or the headline. The conclusion reached requires much stronger evidence not just income tax return data at 30,000 feet level. Why? Here are some reasons:

1. The first issue is treatment of personal income tax data as a proxy for entrepreneurial income is incorrect. India has a large number of closely held businesses structured as small private limited companies, partnerships and LLPs. The way the entrepreneur's returns look is very different.

Profits are taxed at the entity level, and partners often receive exempt profit shares rather than taxable business income. They may deploy those exempt profits into interest/dividend yielding assets and offer only those to tax.

My own case: I run a Private limited company. My return will look like a small salary with higher interest/capital gains income. My return looks like a "Rentier" returns. But my activity is anything but rentier. My returns earlier as a Partner of a professional services firm looked worse. Largely exempt professional income and only "rentier" income.

2. The second issue is the characterization of dividend income as "rentier" or passive income. Dividends received by promoters are fundamentally different from dividends earned by a passive investor holding a diversified stock portfolio. Dividends earned by Shiv Nadar or Azim Premji cannot be called "Rentier" income. And these are big enough to skew the statistics.

3. A third point is that the article appears to equate the "head of income" (a legal concept in income-tax) with its economic substance. Business owners have considerable flexibility in how they extract returns ie salary, dividends, interest, buybacks, partnership profit shares, or leave it as retained earnings. Changes in tax policy, corporate law, or business structures can significantly alter the mix of reported income without indicating any underlying change in entrepreneurial behaviour. Looking only at the labels on tax returns can therefore be misleading.

4. Corporate return or earnings analysis specially to say reduction in industrial sales could be due to housing businesses in subsidiaries and upstreaming income as dividend. Also, overseas expansion through acquisitions or even local acquisition does not show up as sales in Standalone financials including P&L. They show up as treasury income or do not show up as sales at all.

5. Tax return data is at a very high level to do this kind of analysis and arrive at these conclusions. The disclosures of income and heads chosen is a very legal exercise only for the purposes of taxation. Nothing more. It need not be commercial or economic. As an Independent Director... all my directorship fees is included in "other sources" (by law). Other sources is Rentier. But my labour in acting as a director is not!!!

The article confuses the tax classification of income with its economic character. The data may be interesting and is not incorrect, but this is not the strong evidence needed to draw the conclusion that Indian entrepreneurs are increasingly becoming "rentier".

Anecdotally, I can agree with the conclusion also. But I cannot agree that this data proves it.


Roshan Kishore: 1. India’s rich, incl corporates, are increasingly becoming rentiers than entrepreneurs
2. Both tax & corporate earnings data show the rise of rentier incomes rel to profits
3. Its perfectly legal but diverts “animal spirits” towards speculation from growth driving investment

items.title: RT The Indian Express: The Supreme Court on Thursday questioned how the Bihar government could retain Panchayati Raj Minister Deepak Prakash despite h...
items.description_html:
RT The Indian Express
The Supreme Court on Thursday questioned how the Bihar government could retain Panchayati Raj Minister Deepak Prakash despite his remaining unelected beyond the six-month limit prescribed under Article 164(4) of the Constitution.

Hearing a plea challenging Prakash's reappointment, a Bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant asked the state to explain its position, observing, "How are you retaining a minister beyond 6 months when he is not elected?"

The petitioner has argued that Prakash, first sworn in as minister on November 20, 2025, and reappointed on May 7, 2026, after a new council of ministers was formed, could not continue in office without getting elected within the constitutional timeframe. The plea contends that the reappointment circumvents constitutional safeguards and undermines representative democracy.

The Supreme Court said it would not grant the state any more time to file its response and listed the matter for hearing on August 4.

Click the 🔗 below to read the full story.

items.title: RT Mark Zandi: The economy is soft and vulnerable. This is the clear message in today’s GDP, income, and spending data. Abstracting from the vagaries...
items.description_html:
RT Mark Zandi
The economy is soft and vulnerable. This is the clear message in today’s GDP, income, and spending data. Abstracting from the vagaries of the data, real GDP growth is at best 2%, driven largely by AI-related investment and wealth effects that support consumer spending among the well-to-do. But housing, government, and international trade are more or less headwinds to growth. And given that real disposable income is flat and personal savings are about as low as they ever get, spending by middle- and lower-income households is under significant pressure. The longer the Iran war drags on, and the higher energy prices and interest rates go, the more likely these consumers are to pull back – and take the rest of the economy with them.

#WATCH | Mumbai, Maharashtra: Speaking on how much Fed pauses and Bank of Japan moves restrict the RBI's headroom to cut rates in India, CareEdge Ratings Chief Economist Rajani Sinha says, “Given the very fluid macroeconomic environment, we expect the RBI to maintain a status quo in the upcoming meeting. Going forward, the RBI is going to see how the growth and inflation data pans out, and based on that, there could be rate action in the subsequent meetings later in the year. We feel that there are chances of one or two rate hikes later during the year if inflation risks aggravate and if the RBI feels that inflation is becoming broad-based...”

On whether a stronger yen and a high-rate US dollar could spike rupee volatility and slow down FPI inflows, she adds, “Definitely, these concerns exist with the rising US yields and rates going up in Japan. There are concerns around flows to emerging markets, including India. But I would say that right now, there are also favorable factors for India, especially after the RBI announcements for capital flows and the government announcement, which are going to induce more inflows through FIIs. We have already seen FII debt flows of around $8 billion or so in the last two months...”

items.title: There's a lot of discussion about Energy Security. Not enough about Edible oil security. India imports 60% of all our seed oils, and 90% of Palm oils ...
items.description_html:
There's a lot of discussion about Energy Security. Not enough about Edible oil security. India imports 60% of all our seed oils, and 90% of Palm oils (mainly from Malaysia and Indonesia). The largest agri-economy has yet to secure its kitchen oils.

Both Indonesia and Malaysia are now levying export curbs and increasing domestic palm oil blending mandates for domestic energy production. Indonesia is already transitioning from B30 to mandatory B40 and planned B50 biodiesel blending, reducing global export availability. Malaysia is similarly expanding domestic palm oil blending mandates.

Bottomline: There is a massive shift amongst countries towards reducing crude oil imports and blending is the way forward. Ethanol in India, Crude Palm oil (CPO) for them.

Indonesia’s palm oil curbs could open the door for India to step up. What was earlier just an agri-policy (National Mission on Edible Oils) will soon be National priority. And unlike Energy security which is more challenging, this is an easier to solve problem. The acceleration is visible. Telangana and AP have championed the India Palm Oil mission, many more states are coming up now.

Which company fills the void? That's for investors to figure out. A good opportunity in the making.

Read:
https://www.fortuneindia.com/opinion/indonesias-palm-oil-curbs-could-open-the-door-for-india-to-step-up/150389

items.title: The AI memory crash comes on the back of last quarter record profits. Samsung chip division's single-year profits beat its past 40 years total profit....
items.description_html:
The AI memory crash comes on the back of last quarter record profits.

Samsung chip division's single-year profits beat its past 40 years total profit. Last quarter > Last 2 years. Stock has halved in a month.

Micron grew profits by 1400%, stock down 40-45%. Projections talk of record numbers for next 2 years as well. TTM PE hardly 4-5x.

So, why the panic and correction?

1. One obvious reason is profit booking, with record leverage in system amplifying the fall. What unfolded the sell-off was fear - China's Open source model and DRAM buildup fears, bond market pressure etc.

2. The other is valuation mistake. Is trailing P/E the right metric for extraordinary earnings cycle? The risks are in future, not in trail. The lesser variables you have that can impact earnings visibility the better. Here, there are more than what an analyst can predict with confidence.

Is this a buying opportunity? Is there more correction left? I don't know. But I know that basing investment decision solely on the fall from peak is often a mistake.

#FearandGreed

items.title: RT James E. Thorne: Memory Liquidation The AI memory market is not the telecom boom, and it is not the housing bubble. What we are seeing now is a lev...
items.description_html:
RT James E. Thorne
Memory Liquidation

The AI memory market is not the telecom boom, and it is not the housing bubble.

What we are seeing now is a leverage event: too much leverage, too much crowding, and too much exposure piled into the same trade, all of which now need to be unwound. That matters because a real supply crunch in memory has been amplified by positioning, acute shortages and sharply higher prices tied to AI infrastructure demand are real.

Yes the easy money in the AI trade has been made!

Let’s be explicit about what that means. Parabolic charts are not proof of durable fundamentals; they are often evidence of momentum, leverage, and borrowed conviction feeding on themselves. When a trade gets this crowded, price stops reflecting only supply and demand and starts reflecting how much fast money is trapped in the move.

The underlying AI demand story is still real, and the fundamental supply-demand imbalance still exists. AI demand has forced companies to fight for dwindling memory supplies, while chipmakers prioritized higher-margin data-center chips and memory prices spiked sharply over the past year.

But that does not mean every price swing is fundamental. Narrative follows price: when memory names surge, investors discover scarcity; when they break, they suddenly discover China risk or efficiency gains.

That is why the analogies to the 1990s telecom boom and the housing bubble are only partly useful. In those episodes, supply ran ahead of demand, too much fiber, too many houses. Here, demand has outrun supply, but the stock market layered excessive leverage on top of a real bottleneck.

As Graham observed, the market is a voting machine in the short term and a weighing machine in the long run. Right now, the vote is being driven by crowding, leverage, and forced selling.

Over time, the market will weigh the underlying AI demand and the still-tight supply picture on their merits. What is being liquidated is not the existence of demand. It is the leverage wrapped around the story.

Yes Parabolic charts that amplify crowded leverage one way bets should be avoided.

Galilei will also invest 180cr in ICE Make via preference shares

Food Processing & Hospitality already contributes 15-20% of ICE Make’s revenue, while commercial freezers account for only 2%, leaving significant headroom to build a larger standardized HoReCa equipment business

Galilei brings established Japanese product technology and has around 30% share of Japan’s domestic commercial-refrigerator production

https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/corporate/ICEMAKE_24072026125113_Outcome_of_Board_Meeting_final_2.pdf

5. Apollo Micro Systems receives Indian Navy approval to develop an Autonomous Underwater Surveillance System

Apollo Micro Systems has received a Make-II Prototype Sanction Order to develop SAVIOR-ASW, an unmanned semi-submersible vessel that can operate for extended periods and use acoustic sensors and AI/ML to detect and classify submarines and other underwater threats

The system would represent a first-of-its-kind indigenous capability in India and marks Apollo’s formal entry into autonomous maritime and underwater warfare systems

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/408de015-8d30-40a5-9dc6-87c5bc839242.pdf

6. Marine Electricals wins orders worth 376cr including a major order from Siemens for power distribution system that will be used in a Hyperscaler data center

https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/corporate/MARINE_24072026133342_Signed_Regulation_30_Bagging_of_Order.pdf

7. Gabriel India enters ADAS and automotive electronics through JV with Korea-based HL Klemove

Gabriel India will acquire a 30% stake in HL Klemove India for around ₹935 crore, while the Korean parent will retain the remaining 70% stake

HL Klemove India manufactures ADAS radars, front cameras, autonomous-driving control units and software, along with automotive electronics such as braking and steering ECUs

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/6df251ee-57b5-48ab-836c-60d324de1105.pdf

8. Sona Comstar enters into a partnership with Japanese firm Densco Corporation

Sona Comstar and DENSO will establish two India based joint ventures to develop and manufacture traction motors, inverters, generators and eAxles for electric and hybrid vehicles

The first JV will focus on high voltage liquid cooled powertrain systems for passenger and commercial vehicles, with DENSO holding 51% and Sona Comstar holding 49%. This gives Sona access to DENSO’s inverter and hybrid technology and expands it beyond individual EV components into integrated powertrain systems.

In the second JV, Sona will transfer its existing two-wheeler and three-wheeler electric motor and controller business into a subsidiary. DENSO will acquire a 49% stake at an enterprise valuation of ₹1,750 crore, while Sona retains 51% and management control.

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/79c5700d-fea7-4065-9651-2c9e1365c5db.pdf

9. Indo Tech Transformers enters the 400 kV transformer segment for BESS projects

Indo Tech has received NTPC approval to manufacture 400 kV class transformers for BESS projects, expanding its product portfolio beyond the existing 220 kV range
It has also secured an initial order for two 90 MVA, 400 kV transformers through an EPC contractor

Large grid scale BESS projects require high voltage transformers to connect battery systems to 220 kV and 400 kV transmission networks
NTPC’s recent renewable and BESS tenders include 400/33 kV tie transformers and 400 kV pooling substations

The approval moves Indo Tech into a more technically demanding and higher-value transformer segment and positions it to participate in NTPC’s growing BESS and renewable power evacuation pipeline

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/b7377360-48aa-48ed-a80b-86a90e9b668e.pdf

10. Azad Engineering delivers India’s first indigenous 350 kg thrust class expendable turbojet engine

Azad has manufactured and assembled a 350 kg thrust class turbojet engine designed by DRDO’s Gas Turbine Research Establishment, and delivered the first unit to DRDO

This is not a fighter aircraft engine, it is built for a one time use defence platform, such as a missile or unmanned system, rather than a reusable aircraft

The development is significant because Azad is moving beyond manufacturing individual aerospace components to the complete assembly of an indigenous jet engine, establishing system level manufacturing capabilities in a technology mastered by only a few countries

items.description_html:
🚨 C2C’s auditor has issued a qualified opinion and flagged multiple serious financial and compliance concerns:

1️⃣ Liquidity & Going Concern Risk:
The company is facing a liquidity crisis, with statutory dues unpaid due to lack of funds. Recovery from trade receivables remains uncertain, while operations are heavily dependent on short-term promoter funding. The auditor has raised doubt over C2C’s ability to continue as a going concern. Liquidation Risk

2️⃣ CSR Payments Not Cleared:
CSR expenses were recognised through cheques, creating a book overdraft. However, the cheques were not presented for payment. The auditor noted that the CSR obligation is discharged only when the payment is actually cleared.

3️⃣ Statutory Dues Pending:
Undisputed statutory payments remain unpaid. No provision has been made for possible interest or penalties. Delays in filing statutory returns and weak internal controls were also highlighted.

4️⃣ Labour Code Impact Not Assessed:
The company has not quantified the potential impact of new labour regulations on gratuity, provident fund, wages and other employee benefits.

5️⃣ FEMA Compliance Issues:
Overseas receivables remain unrealised beyond RBI timelines. Applications for regularisation are pending, SOFTEX registration is yet to be approved, and possible penalties have not been provided for.

items.title: We initiated Sansera for our subscribers around 16th December 2025. But the more important thing is how we filtered on this idea. > First key factor w...
items.description_html:
We initiated Sansera for our subscribers around 16th December 2025.

But the more important thing is how we filtered on this idea.

> First key factor we observed was the product mix change, where the company's intent was to gradually move from its ICE component business to Aero/Defence/Semicon (ADS) business.

> This product mix shift was visible from the fact that margins had been improving over the last 2 quarters, and growth was starting to pick up. That's how it came under our filters.

> Going a little deeper, we understood that the kind of things it was doing in the ADS business were quite moated. It had a single-source monopoly on Airbus A350/A320 thrust-reversal gimbals with zero defects over 12 years; hogging (machining from solid billet vs. forging) is a much harder-to-replicate capability for aerospace tolerances.

> Also, in its semiconductor business, it was working with Lam Research, where this year their business is expected to go from $10M to $30M .

> Also, as per our channel checks, they had orders/interest from Rolls-Royce for aero-engine feelers, the MMRFIC JV (navy fuses, radars), and a Tesla ESS order.

> All these things were a confirmation of our thesis that management has the capabilities, and that the product mix is changing for good.

> They have also given strong guidance of ₹8,000 Cr in revenue, with ADS at 20–25% of overall business and blended EBITDA margins moving above the 20% mark.

On top of this, we also visited their facility, where we got to understand the manufacturing complexity involved in the components they make for their ADS business, and their capabilities in precision engineering.

The framework was simple: through scanning, found a business where earnings were breaking out and margins were improving > went through their earnings calls and found the story of the product mix change > mapped out the value chain and tried to understand Sansera's moat in the new business they were focusing on > visited their facility to verify our thesis on the company.

Disclaimer: This is not a recommendation to buy or sell. We continue to hold it in our recommendation portfolio and may change our view at any point in time.

RT Sridhar Vembu
Last week, I was fortunate to visit the workshop (the Tamil word pattarai பட்டறை is so appropriate) of the leading motor designer in the world Morihiro Saito-san.

Saito-san is 80+ and still designing advanced motors, some of the most advanced in the world. His modest looking workshop is right next door to a company that builds out those motors in prototype quantities and he works closely with them to get them built. I visited as an industrial "pilgrim", with as much devotion as I go to the Thoranamalai Murugan Temple at home. When I saw him at work, I was moved to touch his feet.

Saito-san, the God of motors, is how Japan is able to retain its global prominence in so many foundational industries.

We need to learn from that spirit. We need to revive our "pattarai" culture of building things - every village in India needs such workshops!

My industrial pilgrimage to Japan has given me new vigor 🙏

items.title: An elevator pitch on how the industrial gases industry works! You separate air into gases, or you buy rare gases and repackage them. You sell either f...
items.description_html:
An elevator pitch on how the industrial gases industry works!

You separate air into gases, or you buy rare gases and repackage them. You sell either from a plant you own (merchant) or from a plant you build inside a customer's factory (on-site).

On-site is a 15-20 year annuity at thin margins. A merchant is a spot market where the same molecule earns very different money depending on the gas, the distance, and who else is selling nearby.

The whole game is capital, location, and the ability to squeeze extra high-margin gas (argon, liquid) out of a plant you've already built.

But let’s get into interesting details about that -

What does the industry actually sell?

Strip away the chemistry and this is an air-separation business. A cryogenic plant is an Air Separation Unit, or ASU that chills atmospheric air until its components liquefy at their different boiling points, and pipes off oxygen, nitrogen and argon at high purity. Everyone in the industry runs broadly the same technology, so purity differences are marginal (roughly plus-or-minus 5%). The molecule is a commodity. Almost everything interesting happens around the molecule in how it's contracted, delivered, and priced.

The demand base has historically been the heavy stuff: steel and metals, autos, pharma, healthcare, and a thin slice of chemicals and F&B. What's changing the growth story is the sunrise demand from solar and semiconductors, which pull large volumes of nitrogen and, in semis, demand purity that cheaper suppliers struggle to hit. That single shift is why every player in the country is pouring capital into new capacity at the same time.

The top four global MNCs Linde, INOX Air Products, Air Water India and Air Liquide India control roughly 80% of the market.

Below them sit regional, owner-driven players (Ellenbarrie, Vayu, Shree Ram Oxygas and similar) who have been around 10–15 years and whose space widened after COVID, when oxygen subsidies pulled local capital in.

Now let’s understand the 2 engines in this industry separately > on-site vs merchant

Everything downstream flows from one fork in the road: do you build the plant inside the customer's factory, or near a cluster of customers and truck the gas out? These are two genuinely different businesses with different economics, different customers, and different personalities.

> On-site - An anchor customer, usually a large steel plant, issues an RFQ saying, in effect, we need ~1,100–1,800 tonnes of gas a day flowing into our furnace. A supplier builds and operates an ASU on their premises under a Build-Own-Operate (BOO) contract running 15–20 years. The revenue is fixed and stable, so it's underwritten on a modest return — players will accept an operating margin of roughly 10–12%, sometimes pricing the whole thing to a ~10–15% IRR. It is deliberately boring money.

Why fight so hard for boring money? Because it's stable, long-dated and defensive with a 15–20 year foothold that also keeps a rival out of that customer. Contracts signed before roughly 2016–18 carried fatter margins and some still run (a few end around 2035), but the new-build market is now openly competitive on price.

> Merchant business - Here you own the plant, liquefy the output, and sell it as liquid, bulk or cylinders to whoever's within reach. Margins are structurally better but volatile: liquid/bulk runs a ~20–25% bottom line, while cylinder and specialty can reach ~40%. The catch is geography. Oxygen and nitrogen are cheap and heavy, so you can't economically truck them much beyond ~200–300 km before distribution cost (typically 10–12% of revenue) eats you alive. You plant an ASU, draw a 200–300 km radius, and fight for that circle.

The reason branded MNCs earn ~40–45% at the top while a strong regional player earns ~35% isn't a secret formula rather it's scale and mix. A Linde or INOX moves 4,000–5,000 TPD daily; a regional player moves 250–300 TPD. At a small scale, tender-driven medical demand keeps margins decent. But to scale from 300 TPD to 3,000–4,000 TPD you must chase the lower-margin sectors that make up the bulk of the market and that's exactly where pricing and margin pressure begin.

The value chain, end to end

Follow a molecule of oxygen from the atmosphere to the customer and you can see where value is captured and where it leaks.

Stage 1 - Build the plant (the capital gate)
This is a capital-intensive, power-intensive industry, and the entry cost is the first moat. A modest 200–250 TPD on-site plant needs at least INR 300–400 crore of initial capex. Core components are compressors, cold boxes that have to be imported; India makes none of them. Only fabrication and storage tanks (INOX, Cryolor, VRV) are domestic. Build time runs 16–24 months per ASU

Stage 2 - Choose your engineering partner (the quiet moat)
Who actually builds the plant is becoming the real differentiator. The MNCs carry in-house EPC muscle - Linde has Linde Engineering, INOX leans on Air Products' US technology which lets them build large, reliable ASUs and win the technically demanding jobs.
Regional players without that engineering wing increasingly tie up with Chinese OEMs on a sale-of-equipment basis: the Chinese firm builds and exits, and the local player does the O&M. It's cheaper (a 200 TPD plant runs ~INR 100–120 crore via a Chinese vendor vs ~INR 150–200 crore via an MNC), but blue-chip steelmakers (Tata, JSW, SAIL, AM/NS) often won't allow a Chinese machine where they're underwriting 15–20 years of reliability, power efficiency and capital backup, and they pay up for it.

The cost-vs-capability gap
> MNC plant, 200 TPD: ~INR 150–200 crore — technology, reliability, blue-chip acceptance.
> Chinese plant, 200 TPD: ~INR 100–120 crore — cost-optimised, favoured by smaller / secondary steel and rolling mills.
> No Indian regulation restricts Chinese ASUs, so the split is driven purely by which customer is buying.

Stage 3 - Extract the by-products (where margin hides)
A basic ASU makes oxygen and nitrogen. To pull argon you must bolt on a separate argon-recovery column and here's the quirk: that column costs roughly the same whether the plant is small or large, but a small 200 TPD ASU yields only ~5–6 TPD of argon while a big ASU yields 50–60 TPD. The capital-to-recovery maths favours scale heavily, yet argon's economics are so attractive that even smaller players are now installing the column anyway.

Stage 4 - Distribute (the tyranny of distance)
Oxygen and nitrogen are regional products which are heavy, cheap, and uneconomic beyond ~300 km. Argon is a national product valuable enough to ship across the country, though distribution then runs ~17–18% of revenue rather than 10–12%. This distinction quietly shapes the entire competitive map: oxygen/nitrogen competition is local and radius-bound, while argon competition is national and cyclical.

How to judge any player in this industry?
Pulling the mechanics together, a handful of questions separate a structurally strong operator from a fragile one regardless of the name on the door.

> Capacity trajectory: Can they actually double liquid capacity? You can't sell a molecule if you can't make expansion of 200 TPD takes 1.5 - 2 years, not six months.

> Mix quality: How much on-site annuity vs volatile merchant? How much argon and by-product upside are they extracting per plant?

> Engineering independence: In-house EPC, or dependent on Chinese OEMs who build and exit? This gates which customers they can win.

> Geographic competition: Are their plants in pockets with few rivals inside the 300 km radius, or in contested western/central India?

> Blue-chip acceptance: Can they clear the reliability/purity bar for Tata, JSW, AM/NS, and semiconductors or are they confined to secondary, cost-driven demand?

> Cycle timing: Are they adding capacity into the current glut, and can their balance sheet and geography absorb 2–3 years of merchant price erosion before demand catches up?

Dislaimer - not a recommendation to buy/sell

items.description_html:
Creative Newtech has done an interesting acquisition, transforming from a distributor to a manufacturer of an integrated surveillance technology platform.

Creative Newtech has approved the acquisition of 100% of Infinova (India) for up to US$4 million, marking a strategic shift beyond distribution into surveillance technology manufacturing.

The acquisition brings Infinova's India operations, brand rights, technical expertise, experienced workforce, and local assembly & manufacturing facility, providing Creative Newtech with immediate execution capabilities.

More importantly, the deal lays the foundation for a 'Make in India' surveillance platform, enabling the company to build proprietary products, strengthen after-sales support, and reduce dependence on third-party distribution.

The transaction also accelerates Creative's transition from a distribution-led business to an integrated, technology-led surveillance solutions provider, giving it greater control over manufacturing, product ownership, and margins.

The company holds all the relevant licenses from Gem, BIS, and STQC, enabling it to access the government portal. STQC shifts 22% market share from Chinese to Indian brands

This is more than an acquisition—it is a business model transformation, positioning Creative Newtech to move up the value chain from distributing surveillance products to designing, assembling, and manufacturing them under a 'Make in India' strategy.

Creative NewTech trades at 18 PE vs Prizor Vtech 42PE vs Aditya Infotech 110PE

Great Punjabi Lala Jagat Narain.
He spent years in prison for opposing both British rule and the Emergency. He built Punjab Kesari into one of Punjab's most widely read newspapers and refused to bow before terror.

He stood up to Bhindranwale despite repeated threats. He was assassinated for his courage. The sacrifices did not end there-his son, Ramesh Chander, was also killed, along with 52 members of the Punjab Kesari family.

The media group lost:
• 2 Editors
• 7 Reporters
• 20 Distribution Agents
• 23 Hawkers
• 2 Workers

Their only "crime" was refusing to surrender to Khalistani intimidation and continuing to print the truth.

Punjab Kesari also raised funds and supported the families of Hindu and Sikh civilians murdered by Khalistani terrorists when the state had largely failed them.

When fear forced distributors to stop carrying the newspaper, KPS Gill ensured copies were distributed through police stations so the voice of truth would not be silenced.

Lala Jagat Narain, the Punjab Kesari family, and KPS Gill remind us that Punjab was saved not only by brave security personnel but also by fearless journalists and ordinary citizens who refused to bow before terror.

Their sacrifice must never be forgotten. 🇮🇳

items.title: RT Sann: His name is Dinesh Thakur. He gave up a safe, high paying job and spent eight years of his life fighting one of the largest drug companies in...
items.description_html:
RT Sann
His name is Dinesh Thakur.

He gave up a safe, high paying job and spent eight years of his life fighting one of the largest drug companies in the country. He did it because he discovered that the medicines millions of people trusted were built on a lie.

He was a chemical engineer who had worked in America and come back to India for a senior role at Ranbaxy, then the biggest generic medicine maker in the country. It was a proud Indian company whose cheap medicines were sold across the world.

Not long after he joined, he was asked to look into the quality of the company's drugs. What he found frightened him.

The company was faking its test results. Medicines were being sold without being properly tested for whether they were safe, or whether they even worked. The data handed to regulators was simply invented.

These were not luxury goods. These were the tablets that sick people swallowed every day, trusting that they would heal them.

Thakur went to his own bosses with what he had found. Nothing changed. So he made a choice that cost him everything. He resigned, and he reported the company to the American drug regulators.

Then began eight long years. He handed over evidence, sat through investigation after investigation, and lived under the shadow of taking on a giant that had every reason to crush him.

In 2013, it ended. Ranbaxy admitted its guilt in an American court, pleaded guilty to seven serious crimes, and was made to pay one of the largest fines ever handed to a generic drug maker, five hundred million dollars.

Because one man refused to look away, the way the world checks the safety of its medicines was changed for good.

He had a comfortable life and a good salary. He gave it all up so that the medicine in a stranger's hand could be trusted.

Why NEW is a powerful word in investing

New Earnings Power. A sharp acceleration in current quarterly EPS/sales vs. the same quarter last year. Not just growth but a new level of earnings the company hasn't printed before.

ANew Earnings Run-Rate. Annual earnings inflecting onto a higher trajectory (and here's where your New Margin Run-Rate fits perfectly — margin expansion driving a structurally higher profit pool, not a one-off).

New Products / New Management / New Highs. The original "N," untouched. The catalyst: a new product, new leadership, new capacity, new addressable market culminating in the stock making new price highs.

New Supply-Demand Setup. A new scarcity in the float: buybacks, low/shrinking share count, tightening supply against rising demand.

New Market Leaders. Buy the relative-strength leaders, not the laggards — the names showing new leadership within their group.

New Institutional Owners. Fresh, high-quality institutional sponsorship coming in & new funds building positions, not stale holders.

New Market Trend. The general market itself turning into a new uptrend (since 3 of 4 stocks follow the market).

items.title: RT Sagar Awatade: I don't know who else to tell this to, so I am going to tell my story here. Every day is a struggle for a young business, but the la...
items.description_html:
RT Sagar Awatade
I don't know who else to tell this to, so I am going to tell my story here.

Every day is a struggle for a young business, but the last few months have been harder than usual.

We are a small Indian company. For more than ten years we have been building a homegrown brand in a product category dominated by big foreign players.

There are almost no Indian names in this space. We set out to be one.

We started in 2014. Over the years we began making parts in India instead of just importing, and we started selling in the US, Dubai, Nepal, Malaysia and South Africa.

We showed up at global trade fairs to represent an Indian brand on the world stage.

In 2023 we changed the import code we use for our product. We did not do this quietly. Every shipment was declared. Nothing was hidden. We didn't invent our approach.

We followed written professional advice and the way this product is treated in markets around the world.

And now we are facing a government demand running into tens of crores in duty recovery and penalties, plus personal penalties on the founders and even on an employee.

For a company our size, this is not a fine we can pay and move on from. This ends us.

We have not run from any of this. I am not built like that. It is not how I was raised. We have written to the authorities, met officials in person, and we have now filed a writ in the High Court.

All we are asking for is a fair treatment.

I set out to build in India and sell to the world. I am asking only that the system back honest founders trying to compete globally, instead of breaking them.

The process is the process, and it exists for a reason. But process should not feel like punishment.

From where I am standing today, it does.
I am not giving up. I have worked too hard for this. If you have read this far, please share it. If you know someone who can help, point them my way. Help me get the word out.

items.description_html: A lot of defense to IT SIs right now is based on assumption that enterprise clients will not open their systems, data & processes to external AI solutions (Claude, OpenAi). However, this defense collapses the moment we have a precedence from a big enterprise opening up just the way enterprises opened up to cloud after a decade long friction. The moment this starts happening, the JVs OpenAi & Claude have formed will make a killing. And, what will take this wall down? For e.g., enterprises are currently very upset after SAP API policy that prohibited clients from using their own data & sending it to external tools via APIs to architect a solution outside of SAP. This can be the 1st hammer in the wall. One wrong step & clients will find ways to disconnect with enterprise OEMs & will be willing to trust(with an agreement perhaps) likes of Claude & OpenAi. The moment this happens, it is done!! This is the biggest risk I foresee.

items.title: Exactly 10 years ago in May 2016, i went to a session on bootstrapping at TiE event in Santa Clara. That changed my life. When i spent time in bay are...
items.description_html:
Exactly 10 years ago in May 2016, i went to a session on bootstrapping at TiE event in Santa Clara. That changed my life.

When i spent time in bay area working on advanced sensing technologies in semicon space, everything was there in life(money, granted patents, travelling to new country every month, wife, so called good life) but it still felt empty within.

Was burning a lot of midnight oil trying to build something, failed twice trying to build in US. Those failures hit hard and made me realise that everthing that i had was only beacuse of the company that i was working for, i was zero outside of it.

During this phase is when i first met @svembu ji, did not know who he was, did not know about zoho. He was wearing a plain simple green kurtha, jeans and slippers gving a session on bootstraping his company. I asked "can we bootstrap a hardware business too ?" And he said " why not ? "

This along with zoho story, made my conviction of moving back to India stronger, it took almost a week for me to digest what zoho was and what was built without raising a single dime from VCs and i felt so proud and blessed to have met the man behind.

Moved back to India same year in October. It was only about building something here which makes sense in long term, something which was ignored by people for a long time.

Ofcourse it came at a cost, divorce, hard time telling people not to worry about me or my personal life, making sure that my parents are not suffering, isolating all the peronal stuff with the vision of building strong electronics manufacutring ecosystem in India.

10 years FF- we are a strong team of 200+, bootstrapped, growing fast, building factories in India which can compete globally soon. On a personal level, i still hardly spend few thousand rupess everymonth, lead a minimal life, have a loving wife who belives in me and a kid who is growing fast, parents who are proud that i am doing something in India.

There is no multimillion dollars in my bank as safety, my kid and wife are Indians with Indian passport and my parents were teachers/avg govt employee without any background in business.

I dont feel empty inside me, anymore. Fire inside me is for building India's electronics manufacturing capacity that can compete globally, a strong ecosystem for next gen to build products from India and a strong team that can run this beyond me.

Jai Hind!🇮🇳

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.description_html: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely rare to see the Mid & Small cap indices (avg of the two) beating the Nifty 50 near the bottom of the cycle. Their avg CAGR has outperformed during the last two tough years as well as all the below trailing years. I am not that surprised as their balance sheet, P&L and cash flow quality has substantially improved post COVID. I believe the biggest multi-baggers will emerge from this space as the earnings growth differential will be significant going forward. Because of the quality differential today vs during pre-COVID period, I would be surprised if their valuations correct to levels seen during the previous crashes. We probably have the best corporate quality and least stressed financials currently compared to any other previous big crisis.

items.title: RT Anil Agarwal: It is painful to see India face the adverse consequences of a war we have nothing to do with, particularly because of raw material se...
items.description_html:
RT Anil Agarwal
It is painful to see India face the adverse consequences of a war we have nothing to do with, particularly because of raw material security. We don’t have to import 90% of our oil, or 95% of our copper or 99.5% of our gold or any other metal resources. Mother Earth has given us the best geology. Last 40 years of practice in the minerals, metals and oil industry have taught me this. Now is the time, with this positive government, to give entrepreneurs freedom.

At just 19, I came to Bombay from Bihar and built a company in this industry from scratch. Vedanta was able to acquire Hindustan Zinc and BALCO under a privatisation programme which was never completed. 26% and 49% stakes are still held by the government and not been transferred as per a predetermined agreement. Vedanta also acquired ONGC Oil and Gas asset via UK’s Cairn and Sesa Goa Iron ore from Japan’s Mitsui.

In each one, the ambition and goal was to increase the production so much that India wouldn’t need to import but, in fact export. In Hindustan Zinc and BALCO, we succeeded. We increased zinc production 10 times, 20 times in aluminium. In the process, more than 1,000 companies have come up for processing this raw material. And Vedanta has contributed Rs 4.5 lakh crore to the exchequer in the last ten years. In oil and gas, our vision is to produce 1 million barrels per day. In iron ore, my vision is to produce 100 million tonnes, 33% of today’s production level. There are many more underperforming government assets that can perform the same way.

Three or four decades ago, there was no know-how, no experts, no finance in this industry. It took a lot of determination. Vedanta raised 35 billion USD from abroad and invested in India. It brought experts and technology. Because of that, Hindustan Zinc can also produce silver and fertiliser, and we are working very hard to start producing critical minerals very soon, something we were told would never happen in India.

Globally, only few very large companies engage in mining as it is very difficult without scale. Vedanta should be for India what Rio Tinto and BHP are for Australia or Vale is for Brazil. Other entrepreneurs and companies must create new Vedantas.

Most of the advanced countries have become prosperous by developing natural resources, including oil and gas. In India, the system has to stop creating hurdles. It needs to take a long-term view, as this government is not revenue-minded but, production-minded. It must facilitate. Instead of notices and judicial activity, all businesses need to receive recognition and respect. Benefit of doubt should pass onto them.

In India, we have economic heroes who can raise production equal to the biggest and best in the world. We should not allow tunnel vision or outdated mindset to keep us small and dependent. Some may remember the case of Rio Tinto which had invested in a diamond mine in Madhya Pradesh. It could have made India a global hub for diamond production, but they exited because of a complex, interfering and discouraging system.

The most important thing is trust. Keep the system simple, keep regulation limited and you eliminate the root cause of wrongdoing. We should have self-certification instead of lengthy approvals and clearances. The Government issues the rulebook and entrepreneurs strictly comply, subject to audit. Constant enquiry and interference only discourage enterprise. Also, the mindset of discrimination between public sector and private sector should change.

This year my family had the biggest tragedy. It was heartening to hear the words of the Prime Minister who said, “You must stay strong and continue to do work which is important for India.” That is the motivation of my life. I have the blessings of my grandfather and grandmother, who spent 40 years in Vrindavan in a small hut, in Manav Seva Sangh with their guruji, Swami Sharnanand Ji Maharaj. They always advised me, if you have wealth, you must use it for society. If you don’t have wealth, you must always help society with your hand. We all are willing to work hard, take risks and ensure that India becomes self-sufficient. The system should encourage us to deliver for our society and nation; this will eradicate unemployment and encourage women empowerment. This sector has given the maximum revenue to the exchequer in India and in the world for nation-building. It will help in making our country a developed nation, as envisioned by our Prime Minister. Let’s make India & Indians proud.

items.title: As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/Mar...
items.description_html:
As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/March trough—are not an exception; they are a recurring feature of market cycles. Just as consistently, these phases have been followed by sharp recoveries once the market establishes a bottom in February or March.
Current sentiment is such that investors are overly focused on the negatives, making the environment appear so foggy that positives have become invisible. This fog, as always, will eventually lift.

While market bottoms and the depth of drawdowns can never be predicted, it is highly probable that market levels a few months from now will be disproportionately higher. Unfortunately, short-term declines are unsettling for investors, causing many to step aside and miss the eventual strong upswing.

In hindsight, this phase will look like an obvious opportunity. But while living through it, investors see only risks and landmines—never the runway for the next flight
